study.title: Psalm 104 The Creator God, Provider and Sovereign
study.overview: This psalm is a hymn to the greatness of God in creation and providence. The psalmist contemplates the order of the world, the dependence of all creatures of divine sustenance and the wisdom with which the Lord governs time, the earth and the sea. The poem begins and ends with personal call to worship, showing that the contemplation of creation must lead to praise. At the same time, the psalm states that God removes evil, preserves life and will renew the earth by its breath.

outline.title: The majesty of the Lord above creation
outline.explanation: The psalmist begins by calling on his own soul to bless the Lord. God is presented as clothed with glory, light, and majesty. The verses describe the sky, the clouds, the wind, the messengers, the land, and the control of God over the chaotic waters. Creation appears as a work ordained by the sovereign word of the Lord, which limits the sea and establishes the stability of the earth.

outline.title: God provides water, food, and shelter for creatures
outline.explanation: In this part, the focus goes from the cosmic order to concrete care for living beings. Sources, rivers, rain, vegetation, bread, wine and olive oil show God as a provider. Birds, animals of the field and even the tall and rocky places have provision and refuge prepared by it. The psalm highlights the interdependence between creation and divine sustenance.

outline.title: Times, night, work and life renewal
outline.explanation: The moon and the sun regulate the times and rhythms of life. The night serves wild animals and the day to human work. The psalmist then celebrates the wisdom of God in the works of the earth and the sea, including the beings of the great sea and the Leviathan. Everything depends on the food given by God, his breath and his open hand; without it, life returns to dust, and with this the earth is renewed.

outline.title: Final praise, fear and separation between just and ungodly
outline.explanation: The closing affirms the permanence of the glory of the Lord and its contentment in the works he has done. The earth trembles before his gaze and touches, while the psalmist commits to singing and meditating on it for life. The end of the psalm declares that sinners will be removed from the earth, concluding with a final call for the soul to bless the Lord.

study.context: The notes received treat this psalm as a hymn of creation, in close relation to other psalms of praise. Matthew Henry observes that he begins and ends with the same summon: "Bendize, O my soul, to the Lord." Tyndale points out that the psalmist contemplates the present creation, the original creation and a future creation. The notes also point to a contrast to ancient deities linked to the sea, affirming the Lord's sovereignty over the waters. There are, however, no historical data detailed in the notes on date, location or specific compositional circumstances.
study.theology: The psalm teaches that God is at the same time transcendent and close: he is clothed with majesty, but also sustains every creature with food, water and breath. Creation is not independent; it lives from God's continuous providence. There is here a theological vision of order: the world is wise, organized and full of goods because it is from the wise Lord. The psalm also affirms the moral seriousness of creation: evil will not have the final word, for sinners will be consumed and the glory of the Lord will remain forever. The renewal of the earth by the divine breath suggests that life is God's gift from beginning to end, and that correct worship is born from the contemplation of his work.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm is a hymn of creation that contemplates the present world, the original creation and a future new creation, all as works of the Spirit of the Lord.
The psalmist begins his meditation with a personal call to his own soul to worship, showing that praise should involve all faculties.
The greatness and majesty of God manifest themselves in the works of creation; for ordinary minds, they provide strong proof of the divine being and attributes.

questions: What changes in our reading of the world when we see it as a wise and provident work of God, and not as something autonomous?
In which areas of life have I forgotten that even food, water, work and rest depend on the Lord's open hand?
Does my worship end in intellectual admiration or lead me, as the psalmist, to a personal commitment and persevering of praise?
study.practice: Set a time to read the psalm slowly and identify, verse by verse, how God sustains life today: water, food, work, rest, time and breath. Then turn these observations into concrete prayer, thanking you for specific provisions. It is also worth practicing humility: when perceiving the order of creation, reject the idea that everything depends only on human effort. Finally, make praise a daily habit, not just a momentary emotional response.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not bring secure information about authorship, date, location or specific historical context of the psalm, so the study should not treat them as established facts. The expression "Leviathan" appears in the notes only as a creature of the sea, without additional symbolic deepening authorized. There is also no basis in the notes to accurately define a detailed eschatological interpretation of the final verses; therefore, the reference to the judgment on the wicked should be read in a sober way, according to the text itself and the commentators cited.
